'''Jill Annette Ovens'''<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ilo.org/asia/events/WCMS_099341/lang--en/index.htm |title=List of Participants |website=[[International Labour Organization]] |date=19 May 2008 |access-date=17 December 2023 |language=en }}</ref> is a New Zealand trade unionist, politician, and [[anti-transgender]] activist. She is the founder and current national secretary of the Women's Rights Party.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The New Zealand health system has been distracted by a radical gender ideology. |url=https://womensrightsparty.nz/what-women-want/ |access-date=26 May 2023 |website=Women's Rights Party |language=en-US}}</ref> 

She was co-leader of the [[Alliance (New Zealand political party)|Alliance]] party before changing her allegiance to the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]], and then later founding and co-leading the Women's Rights Party.

==Union leader==
Ovens worked as a public relations officers for the [[State Coal Mines Department]] for eight months from mid-1986 while the department was transitioning to be the [[Coal Corporation]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Changeover to Coal Corporation seen as a 'total disaster' |url= https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/CHP19870323.2.27 |access-date=4 November 2023 |work=[[The Press]] |date=23 March 1987 |page=3 }}</ref> Ovens led a group of women in [[Huntly, New Zealand|Huntly]] in response to job losses among coal mine workers. In her role as public relations officer, she organised meetings at a local [[community centre]] where local women coordinated efforts to support the community following the loss of 500 jobs. These meetings also served as a forum for discussing the circumstances of the layoffs, which took place during the transition from State Coal to the Coal Corporation.<ref>{{cite news |title=The way we were |work=[[Waikato Times]] |date=14 March 2012 |page=15 }}</ref> 

Ovens served as the president of the Association of Staff in Tertiary Education (ASTE) and was heavily involved in the [[New Zealand Council of Trade Unions|Council of Trade Unions]] (CTU) Women's Council Convenor and attended the ICFTU World Women's Conference as one of two CTU delegates.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type%3DPeople%26ID%3D2200 |title=Alliance New Zealand |accessdate=6 August 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060206213950/http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=People&ID=2200 |archive-date=6 February 2006 }}</ref>{{When|date=November 2023}} At the 2003 CTU national conference she called on delegates to push for legislative change to improve [[work-life balance]]. Her suggestions for this included moving to a 35-hour working week and legal protections for people in part-time employment.<ref>{{cite news |title=Workplace health and safety must improve, CTU told |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|Dominion Post]] |date=23 October 2003 |page=A5 }}</ref>

In 1999, as national president of the ASTE, Ovens responded to the decision to merge Wellington Polytechnic with [[Massey University]]. The merger included plans to phase out several polytechnic courses. Under Ovens’ leadership, the union opposed the course reductions, citing their role in preparing students for employment-related qualifications. ASTE also advocated for the protection of staff interests during the merger, seeking to ensure the retention of polytechnic tutors and the maintenance of their salaries.<ref>{{cite news |first=Paul |last=Moran |title=Staff fear tech subjects may be at risk |work=[[The Dominion (Wellington)|The Dominion]] |date=27 May 1999 |page=7 }}</ref>

The ASTE opposed a proposal by [[Southern Institute of Technology|Southland Polytechnic]] that would have replaced salary increases with a [[With-profits policy#Types of bonus|bonus scheme]] for tutors. Polytechnic chief executive [[Penny Simmonds]] supported the proposal, stating it was intended to benefit both students and staff, and citing demographic decline and economic uncertainty as reasons for the approach. Simmonds emphasised the need for long-term financial decisions to maintain low student fees and preserve staff positions. Ovens, representing the ASTE, argued that the proposal was inequitable for employees and expressed concern that staff salaries would fall further behind those in the wider sector. Following staff rejection of the offer, a stopwork meeting was held, during which Ovens indicated that industrial action could occur if the polytechnic did not revise its position.<ref>{{cite news |first=Nicky |last=Baird |title=Union rejects bonus plan |work=[[The Southland Times]] |date=3 July 1999 |page=4 }}</ref> Staff subsequently voted to strike, with the union advocating for a 2 percent wage increase in the current year and a similar increase in 2000, in contrast to the proposed $800 bonus and staggered pay adjustments.<ref>{{cite news |first=Nicky |last=Baird |title=Polytech tutors walk out |work=[[The Southland Times]] |date=5 August 1999 |page=3 }}</ref>

In 2001, the Association of Staff in Tertiary Education (ASTE) and 12 polytechnics began discussions to establish a multi-employer collective agreement. A union ballot conducted across the polytechnics indicated strong support for the proposal. Ovens also supported the initiative, noting that many institutions already had identical or similar employment contracts. The introduction of the [[Employment Relations Act 2000]] had made such multi-employer agreements possible.<ref>{{cite news |title=Polytech contract talks |work=[[The Nelson Mail]] |date=8 February 2001 |page=3 }}</ref>

Ovens opposed [[Chosun University]] establishing an English language school at the former Upper Hutt campus of the Central Institute of Technology (CIT). Following the closure of CIT in 2001, Chosun University secured a short-term lease on a section of the campus that had been recently constructed by students from Wellington Polytechnic. Ovens expressed concern that the facilities were being used to benefit international students.<ref>{{cite news |first=Hank |last=Schouten |title=Plan for CIT irks staff group |work=[[The Evening Post (New Zealand)|The Evening Post]] |date=18 March 2002 |page=3 }}</ref>

In late 2002 she was involved in a pay dispute at [[Wellington College of Education]] when industrial action began by lecturers seeking better pay.<ref>{{cite news |title=Lecturers unhappy |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|Dominion Post]] |date=28 October 2002 |page=A9 }}</ref> A month later, after mediation, the lecturers accepted the offer of a 2.5 per cent pay increase.<ref>{{cite news |first=Ann-Marie |last=Johnson |title=Lecturers settle on pay |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|Dominion Post]] |date=20 November 2002 |page=A9 }}</ref>

Since her election to the [[Service & Food Workers Union]], Ovens has been occasionally blogging on social media websites and supporting union activities primarily based in Auckland. In December 2014, Ovens helped lead a walkout of food service workers at [[Auckland City Hospital]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/business/better-business/64164747/Auckland-Hospital-workers-walk-over-outsource-call |title=Auckland Hospital workers walk over outsource call |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=15 December 2014 |accessdate=8 April 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://thedailyblog.co.nz/2014/12/17/guest-blog-jill-ovens-auckland-hospital-worker-cuts-democracy-the-loser/ |title=GUEST BLOG: Jill Ovens – Auckland Hospital worker cuts – Democracy the loser « The Daily Blog |publisher=Thedailyblog.co.nz |date=17 December 2014 |accessdate=8 April 2017}}</ref>

Ovens was co-leader of the Midwifery Employee Representation & Advisory Service (MERAS). After retiring as co-leader, she was the MERAS representative during public service pay adjustment talks in June 2022.<ref>{{cite news |first=Andrea |last=Vance |title=Govt calls deal PSPA, workers call it 'piss-poor' |work=[[Sunday Star-Times]] |date=11 June 2023 |page=2 }}</ref>

==Alliance and Labour activism==
=== Alliance Party===
Ovens was a candidate for the [[Alliance (New Zealand political party)|Alliance]] party in [[Auckland]]'s [[Mount Albert (New Zealand electorate)|Mount Albert electorate]] during the [[1999 New Zealand general election|1999]] and [[2002 New Zealand general election|2002]] general elections, contesting the seat against [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] leader [[Helen Clark]]. On the Alliance party list, she was ranked 28th in 1999 and 12th in 2002.<ref name="Grant">{{cite book |last=Grant |first=David |title=Anderton: His Life and Times |publisher=Te Herenga Waka University Press |year=2022 |isbn=9781776920563 |location=Wellington |ref=Grant}}</ref>{{rp|302}} She was a member of the Alliance council (its governing body) and was involved in internal party efforts opposing New Zealand's participation in the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|War in Afghanistan]].<ref name="Grant" />{{rp|340}} Ovens expressed concerns regarding party leader [[Jim Anderton]]'s leadership approach. During a party conference in November 2001, a debate on Afghanistan was interpreted by Anderton as a leadership challenge, contributing to internal divisions and ultimately leading to Anderton's departure from the party.<ref>{{cite news |first=Ruth |last=Laugesen |title=Anderton ready for next alliance |work=[[Sunday Star-Times]] |date=24 March 2002 |page=A9 }}</ref>

In 2003, Ovens became editor of the political studies journal ''Review of Red & Green: The NZ Journal of Left Alternatives''.<ref>{{citation |url=https://doi.org/10.24135/pjr.v9i1.772 |first=Geraldene |last=Peters |title=REVIEW: New Left journal of analysis in pursuit of another world Review of Red & Green: The NZ Journal of Left Alternatives 1(1), edited by Jill Ovens |journal=[[Pacific Journalism Review]] |volume=9 |issue=1 |year=2003 |doi=10.24135/pjr.v9i1.772 |doi-access=free}}</ref> She stood as a candidate for the [[Auckland Regional Council]] in the Manukau ward during the 2004 local-body elections but was not elected.<ref>{{cite news |title=Local vote: Regional Councils |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/ilocal-votei-regional-councils/SQAAQWI4I6LN2A7FADQG4FNKDQ/ |access-date=11 November 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=11 October 2004 }}</ref>

Ovens became president of the Alliance in 2004.<ref name="switches to Labour" /> She had previously been critical of the party's leader at the time, [[Matt McCarten]], due to his connections with the [[Te Pāti Māori|Māori Party]], including his role in organizing the [[2004 Te Tai Hauauru by-election]] campaign for Māori Party candidate [[Tariana Turia]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Alliance split won't stop party's election plans – president elect |url= https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/alliance-split-wont-stop-partys-election-plans-president-elect/XLKFYFPCYULPHPTJUKQ65FRGPE/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |agency=[[New Zealand Press Association]] |date=5 November 2004}}</ref> Following the by-election, speculation arose regarding a potential merger between the Alliance and the Māori Party. Ovens issued a press statement denying merger talks. <ref name="Poor">{{cite thesis |last=Poor |first=Christopher J. |title=Accountability of Political Party Elites – Intra-party Democratization in The New Zealand Alliance |degree=PhD |publisher=[[University of Auckland]] |url=https://researchspace.auckland.ac.nz/bitstream/handle/2292/61044/Accountability%20of%20Political%20Party%20Elites%3A%20Intra-party%20Democratisation%20in%20the%20New%20Zealand%20Alliance.pdf |year=2005}}</ref>{{rp|77–8}} The Alliance executive committee criticized this statement, leading to the passage of a motion restricting her from making further public comments. Ovens resigned as president, but a group of Auckland-based party members organized a meeting urging her to reconsider. Although Ovens attempted to withdraw her resignation, McCarten informed media that she had resigned, preventing her return to the position.<ref name="Poor" />{{rp|79–80}}  McCarten subsequently resigned from the Alliance in November 2004. At the same conference, Ovens was re-elected president and the party confirmed its intention to run a [[Electoral list|party list]] in the next general election.<ref name="Poor" />{{rp|81}}

For the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 general election]], Ovens contested the [[Manukau East]] electorate and was ranked first on the Alliance party list. She served as co-leader of the party alongside [[Paul Piesse]].<ref name="Grant" />{{rp|373}}  The Alliance campaigned on a [[Socialism|socialist]] platform during that election.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Young |first1=Audrey |title=Alliance pushing unashamedly socialist stance |url= https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/alliance-pushing-unashamedly-socialist-stance/44SHFNRENPD3SW5UI3AYZXR34E/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=7 September 2005}}</ref> In December 2005, it was announced that Ovens had stepped down as co-leader and resumed the role of party president. She was succeeded as co-leader by her husband Len Richards.<ref>{{cite press release |author=<!--Not stated--> |title=Alliance looks to future |url= https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO0512/S00091/alliance-looks-to-future.htm |location= |publisher=[[Alliance (New Zealand political party)|Alliance]] |agency=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]] |date=12 December 2005 |access-date=7 November 2023}}</ref>

===Labour Party===
In 2006, Ovens resigned from the Alliance party.<ref>{{cite web |title=Alliance president resigns over links to Maori Party |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/alliance-president-resigns-over-links-to-maori-party/A4W4GEBDPACXQ66CKT5U63325I/ |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=10 November 2023 |language=en-NZ |date=11 November 2023}}</ref> Following her election as northern secretary of the [[Service & Food Workers Union]]—defeating Lisa Eldret, the preferred successor to former secretary [[Darien Fenton]]—she joined the Labour Party, which is affiliated with the union.<ref name="switches to Labour">{{cite news |last1=Young |first1=Audrey |title=Ovens switches to Labour after winning union vote |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10394898 |accessdate=11 April 2017 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=6 August 2006}}</ref> She later served as the Auckland/Northland regional representative on the Labour Party Council.<ref>{{cite news |title=Party Information |url=http://www.labour.org.nz/party_resources |accessdate=4 August 2017 |work=[[New Zealand Labour Party]] |archive-date=28 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628183932/https://www.labour.org.nz/party_resources |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Ovens stood as a Labour candidate in the [[2013 Auckland local board elections]] for the [[Papakura Local Board]] but was not elected.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/EN/AboutCouncil/HowCouncilWorks/Elections/Documents/2013acelectionfinalresultac.pdf|title=Elections|publisher=[[Auckland Council]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131102012629/http://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/EN/AboutCouncil/HowCouncilWorks/Elections/Documents/2013acelectionfinalresultac.pdf |archive-date=2 November 2013}}</ref> In the [[2022 Auckland local board elections|2022 local board elections]], she again ran as a Labour candidate, this time for the [[Franklin Local Board]] in the Waiuku Subdivision, but was unsuccessful.<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 October 2022 |title=Local elections 2022 – Official results |url=https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/elections/elections-2022-results/results/local-elections-2022-official-results-combined.pdf |access-date=15 October 2022 |website=Local elections 2022 – Official results |publisher=[[Auckland Council]] |archive-date=17 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017061419/https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/elections/elections-2022-results/results/local-elections-2022-official-results-combined.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> 

== Anti-transgender activism ==
In 2021, Ovens submitted testimony opposing the [[Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Act 2022|Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill]]. She argued that the legislation could prevent the use of [[conversion therapy]] on [[transgender youth]], a practice she supported in cases where it aimed to explore alternatives to [[gender transition]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 May 2023 |title=Jill Ovens – New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/sc/submissions-and-advice/document/53SCJU_EVI_113397_JU18124/jill-ovens |access-date=26 May 2023 |website=www.parliament.nz |language=en}}</ref>

=== Women's Rights Party ===
{{redirect|Women's Rights Party|other similarly named parties|Women's Party (disambiguation){{!}}Women's Party}}
In 2023, Ovens resigned from the Labour Party, citing disagreement with the party's support for transgender rights. She then founded the Women's Rights Party, an [[anti-transgender]] party.<ref name="Who's who">{{Cite news |last=Scott |first=Matthew |date=26 September 2023 |title=Who's who in the Election Fringe Festival |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/whos-who-in-the-election-fringe-festival |access-date=23 October 2023 |work=Newsroom |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031203239/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/whos-who-in-the-election-fringe-festival |url-status=live }}</ref> She is the national secretary and co-leader of the party.<ref>{{cite web |title=Jill Ovens |url=https://womensrightsparty.nz/team/jill-ovens/ |publisher=Women's Rights Party |access-date=30 September 2023 }}</ref>

During the [[2023 New Zealand general election]], Ovens was ranked first on the Women's Rights Party's [[party list|list]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Election 2023 Candidates |url=https://womensrightsparty.nz/election-2023-candidates/ |publisher=Women's Rights Party |access-date=29 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929014804/https://womensrightsparty.nz/election-2023-candidates/ |archive-date=29 September 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> The party gained 2,513 votes (0.08%) of the party vote and did not win any seats.<ref>{{cite web |title=2023 General Election – Official Result |url=https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=25 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231122050833/https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |archive-date=22 November 2023 |date=3 November 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Ovens contested the [[2023 Port Waikato by-election]] representing the Women's Rights Party and placed seventh, receiving 188 votes (1% of votes cast).<ref>{{cite web |title=Port Waikato – Official Result |url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/2023_port_waikato_byelection/index.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |date=6 December 2023|access-date=7 December 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207202840/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/2023_port_waikato_byelection/index.html|archive-date=7 December 2023|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=20 October 2023 |title=Port Waikato by-election: Labour won't stand a candidate in 'unwinnable' by-election |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/500630/port-waikato-by-election-labour-won-t-stand-a-candidate-in-unwinnable-by-election |access-date=1 November 2023 |website=[[Radio New Zealand]] |language=en-nz}}</ref>

==Personal life==
As of 2015, Ovens lives in Auckland with her partner Len Richards.<ref>{{cite news |first=Nigel |last=Moffiet |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/auckland/local-news/papakura-courier/71553216/clampdown-on-dogs-excessive---residents |title=Clampdown on dogs excessive – residents |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=1 September 2015 |page=4 November 2023 }}</ref> Sources from 2007 list them as married.<ref>{{cite news |last1=James |first1=Colin |author1-link=Colin James (journalist) |title=How Labour could have invested in new language |url=http://www.colinjames.co.nz/2007/11/06/how-labour-could-have-invested-in-new-language/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |work=colinjames.co.nz |date=6 November 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dye |first1=Stuart |title=I missed him, says megaphone man |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/i-missed-him-says-megaphone-man/VDTUYXU5RDYZA7F42QMAVTPYQY/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=6 November 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=I missed him, says megaphone man |url= https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/labour-delegate-to-be-quizzed-by-police-over-megaphone-assault/7STBQUI5XGZP6L7XUOA27YBKJA/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=18 November 2007 |agency=[[New Zealand Press Association]]}}</ref>
